title: Kimbap
subtitle: Korean rice and vegetable rolls wrapped in nori
excerpt: Kimbap is a Korean rolled dish of seasoned rice, vegetables, egg, and beef wrapped in sheets of dried seaweed. This recipe makes 6 rolls and takes about 50 minutes. It is a staple of Korean picnics and packed lunches, sliced into rounds and served at room temperature.
sourceNotes: Kimbap developed in the late 19th and early 20th century as Korea was influenced by Japanese gimbap during the Japanese colonial period, though the dish has distinct Korean ingredients and seasoning. Korean kimbap uses sesame oil-seasoned rice and traditional fillings such as danmuji (yellow pickled radish), spinach namul, and bulgogi, distinguishing it clearly from Japanese maki sushi.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten within 2 hours of rolling. Do not refrigerate as the rice hardens. If making ahead, wrap the uncut rolls tightly in cling film and slice just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Kimbap, from gim (dried seaweed) and bap (rice), is a Korean rolled dish distinct from Japanese sushi. The rice is seasoned with sesame oil and salt rather than vinegar, giving it a nutty warmth. The fillings are fully cooked before rolling and the roll is eaten at room temperature. Kimbap does not involve raw fish and is a common picnic and lunchbox food in Korea.

Nori is dried and pressed seaweed sheets used across East Asian cooking. In Korean cooking, the sheets used for kimbap are called gim and are lightly roasted. They have a thin, papery texture and a savoury, slightly oceanic flavour. They become pliable when pressed against warm rice, making them easy to roll tightly.

and filled with sesame-seasoned rice, blanched spinach, fried carrots, cucumber, egg strips, and thinly sliced beef. The rolls are sliced into rounds and served at room temperature.

Season the cooked rice with sesame oil and salt while it is still warm, then spread it flat on a tray to cool completely before rolling. Warm rice tears the nori and the roll will not hold together. Each filling should be prepared and cooled before you start assembling. Work with one roll at a time and roll firmly but without crushing the fillings.

content.text: Season the warm cooked rice with 2 teaspoons of sesame oil and half a teaspoon of salt. Mix well, spread onto a tray, and leave to cool to room temperature.
Prepare all fillings: blanch and season the spinach, stir-fry the carrots, cook and slice the egg omelette, and stir-fry the marinated beef. Cool everything fully before rolling.
Place a bamboo rolling mat on a clean surface. Lay one nori sheet shiny-side down on the mat.
With wet hands, spread a thin, even layer of rice across the nori, leaving a 3cm bare strip along the far edge.
Arrange a line of each filling across the centre of the rice in a neat row: spinach, carrots, cucumber, egg strips, and beef.
Lift the near edge of the mat and roll it over the fillings, pressing firmly as you go. Continue rolling until the bare nori edge seals the roll. Press to firm up the shape.
Rub a few drops of sesame oil over the outside of the roll and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Repeat with the remaining rolls.
Slice each roll into rounds about 1.5cm thick using a sharp, lightly oiled knife. Wipe the blade between cuts for clean edges. Serve immediately or within 2 hours.

items.cause: The rice was still warm when the roll was assembled, making the nori soggy and weak
items.fix: Cool the rice completely before spreading. Work quickly once the fillings are placed and roll with confident, even pressure rather than slow hesitant movements

items.symptom: The roll falls apart when sliced
items.cause: The roll was not pressed firmly enough during rolling or the knife was dragged rather than cut cleanly
items.fix: Press each roll firmly along its length before slicing. Use a very sharp knife and a clean, decisive cut, wiping the blade between each slice

items.symptom: The rice is dry and grainy
items.cause: The rice was overcooked or cooled for too long before rolling
items.fix: Season the rice while it is still warm and cover with a damp cloth as it cools. Roll within 30 minutes of cooling for the best texture

content.text: Kimbap is the food Koreans pack for day trips, picnics, and hikes. It is sold at convenience stores across South Korea, wrapped in plastic and ready to eat, and it is the dish many Korean parents make for school trips. It is not eaten as a restaurant meal in the way that many Korean dishes are: it is portable food, made at home and taken somewhere. The fillings vary enormously by family and region. Canned tuna is a common substitute for beef. Yellow pickled radish is a traditional addition. Whatever goes inside, the format is always the same: seasoned rice, varied fillings, nori, rolled and sliced.
